parts.title: Climate Change Helps an Invasive Blowfly Settle In and Thrive in the Polar Regions: What Long-Term Monitoring of Calliphora vicina Shows
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Simple Summary

The sub-Antarctic islands, such as the Kerguelen Islands, are far from anywhere else. Because of this isolation, they are home to a special mix of species. But the same isolation, together with the small number of species that live there, makes these islands easier for newcomers to invade. This matters more and more, because climate change is warming the islands. The warmer weather is making life harder for the local species, and it may be making life easier for species that arrived recently, most of which come from warmer places.

In such a fragile and unusual ecosystem, species that do not belong there are a serious threat. So we need to understand exactly how climate change affects these newcomers, so that we can predict whether their numbers are likely to grow or shrink. In this study, we asked whether warmer temperatures helped a blowfly that does not belong in the islands, Calliphora vicina, settle in and spread across Kerguelen. We found that warming has made this species better able to survive and to breed each year, and that it should keep benefiting as temperatures rise. We also discuss how this invasive blowfly might affect the local ecosystem. We recommend more studies to measure its effects and to find ways to manage it, because this species is likely to stay in the islands for a long time.

Abstract

The isolated sub-Antarctic islands are of great interest to scientists because they hold a unique variety of species and because people have disturbed them very little for a long time. Since Europeans arrived, however, human activity and the species that people brought with them have put more and more pressure on these islands and their sensitive wildlife. In such delicate ecosystems, invasions by species from elsewhere are an exceptional threat, and climate change may make that threat even worse.

We followed the story of the blowfly Calliphora vicina (first described by Robineau-Desvoidy in 1830). It was first brought to the sub-Antarctic Kerguelen Islands in the 1970s. For several decades, people thought it could survive there only in small, sheltered spots where the weather was milder. Here, we show that in recent decades C. vicina has been able to settle in across much more of the islands.

To find out whether warmer conditions help explain how the fly is doing today, and how its numbers rise and fall, in the eastern Kerguelen Islands, we combined two kinds of evidence. First, we ran experiments to measure how temperature affects how fast the fly develops. Second, we used many years of records of the fly's ecology and of the weather. We found that warmer temperatures, and the total amount of warmth built up over the season (measured in "degree days"), could explain both the timing of the fly's yearly life events and how its invasion has unfolded over the long term. This suggests that climate change has likely helped the fly settle in. Our study offers a rare, long-term view of an invader in a polar region, and it highlights how quickly cold regions are becoming easier to invade as the climate changes.

Keywords: biological invasion, sub-Antarctic, Calliphoridae (the blowfly family), climate change, phenology (the timing of seasonal life events), degree day, thermal requirements (the temperatures an animal needs), insect development, ectotherm (an animal whose body temperature follows its surroundings)
parts.introduction_first:
People around the world now carry species to new places and release them there, and this has become a serious problem for nature and for efforts to protect it. Invasive species, meaning living things that spread after being brought to a place where they do not naturally live, are changing communities of plants and animals on land and in water all over the globe [1,2]. Climate change makes these invasions much more dangerous. It helps newcomers settle in, grow in number and spread to new areas in several different ways [3,4]. As a result, more and more studies report that invasions can change how ecosystems work [5,6], which species live together, and the web of who eats whom [7]. This can make communities of species in different places more and more alike, and it can lead to the loss of native species and of endemic species, which are found nowhere else [8].

People often say that climate change is an important reason why newcomers settle in, multiply and spread. Even so, it has often been hard to work out exactly how much climate change adds to an invasion. Other factors can get mixed up with climate and make its effect hard to separate [3,9,10]. These include how many individuals of a species arrive and how often (called "propagule pressure"), how much effort goes into introducing it, and other kinds of global change. In particular, nitrogen falling from the air (often from pollution), pollution more generally, natural areas being broken up into small patches, and changes in how land is used are major forces that drive how invasions happen and what they do [11,12]. This is why polar regions (the Arctic, the sub-Arctic, the Antarctic and the sub-Antarctic) and high mountain areas are so useful for studying how climate change affects the success of invasions. People have damaged the environment less in these places than in other parts of the world.
parts.conclusion:
5. Conclusions

We brought together several kinds of evidence: many years of monitoring the fly in the wild, experiments on how it develops, and weather records. With them, we found a link between warmer temperatures and two things about C. vicina in the Kerguelen Islands: how it settled in over the long term, and how it behaves through the seasons. We have shown that this species is sensitive to climate change and will likely keep benefiting as temperatures rise. It may even come to produce more generations each year.

Until recently, polar ecosystems were left fairly "untouched". Now they face growing pressure from two global problems that act together: climate change and invasions by species from elsewhere. Like other invaders in these ecosystems, C. vicina was brought to the Kerguelen Islands and managed to survive there long enough to benefit from the warming.

This species could have strong effects on the ecosystem, and the Kerguelen Islands are sensitive and unusual. For these reasons, we stress that this population must keep being monitored, and that studies must be done on its role in the web of life on the land in the sub-Antarctic. Getting rid of the fly completely, for example by spraying insecticide, is not possible in this ecosystem, because it would put at risk other small animals without backbones that the spray is not meant for. So we need to find out what effects this species has, so that efforts to manage it can be planned carefully and aimed at the right targets. This can reduce any harm to species and communities that are at risk, and help decide whether action is needed to stop the fly from spreading across the islands.

It is essential to make it a priority to better understand how species brought to cold regions invade, and how their futures are tied to a fast-changing climate. As our technology makes it easier for people to use and exploit polar regions, it also gives invaders more chances to do the same.
parts.introduction_rest:
Small animals without backbones, such as insects, cope poorly with warming, because they cannot make their own body heat and depend on the heat around them. For these animals, two things largely decide where they can live and what range of temperatures suits them: how much heat they can stand, and how much drying out they can survive [13]. In the Antarctic regions, many of these communities already live at the edge of the climate they can cope with. This suggests that as climate change speeds up, these species are likely to face even greater threats and to be pushed out of their homes even further [14].

Weather is also expected to become more changeable. That would threaten animals that can only handle a narrow range of heat and dryness, while favouring those that can handle a wider range. This idea is called the climate variability hypothesis [15], and it applies especially to species that do not belong in a place. Finally, as warming opens up new temperature ranges, polar regions become more suitable for newcomers that are less able to cope with stress. Some species that were already living in these regions may change from simply being present to becoming invasive [4,13].

The new conditions brought by climate change can also help newcomers at the expense of native species, especially in cold regions. In these ecosystems, native species are adapted to the cold, while newcomers are usually adapted to warmer conditions. So rising temperatures may affect the two groups in opposite ways [16,17]. Together, climate change and invasions can pose a serious threat to cold ecosystems.

The timing of seasonal life events, such as when a species hatches, grows or breeds, is thought to be a key sign of how living things respond to climate change [18,19]. As temperatures rise, many groups of living things shift these events earlier in the year. Yet little attention has gone to how useful this timing is for showing which part of the year each species in a community uses. As growing seasons get longer, though, there may be free time in the year that no native species uses, and newcomers could move into it and invade.

More and more, scientists see newcomers as successful invaders because they are often more sensitive to changes in the timing of their seasonal life events than native species are [20]. This lets newcomers take advantage of windows of opportunity in places where the year has become longer and native species cannot keep up with the shifting climate [21]. So the seasonal timing of newcomers, and how sensitive it is to climate, can help us understand whether they can settle in a community.

Climate change matters especially in polar and high mountain regions, where recent warming has been stronger than in other parts of the world [22]. These changes have already caused many groups of living things, on land and in the oceans, to shift where they live towards the poles [19,20]. However, scientists have studied less than in temperate regions how far newcomers have spread or shifted because of climate change in polar regions (but see [23] for an exception).

The climate of the sub-Antarctic is not as cold as that of other polar regions, but it stays cold all year round, from about 2 °C in winter to 8 °C in summer [16]. This can be a challenge for animals whose body temperature follows their surroundings. Temperatures that used to hold newcomers back in this region are now rising, and this could now let them settle in.

The blowfly Calliphora vicina (first described by Robineau-Desvoidy in 1830) lives on every continent except Antarctica. Even though it is found in so many places, most studies of this species have looked at how it develops and at its general biology (for example, see [24]). This is because the fly is useful in forensic entomology, the use of insects to help solve crimes, such as working out when a body died (for example, [25,26]). As a result, we know very little about how it behaves as an invader or what effects it has on nature [27].

Other invasive blowflies, however, are known to harm native species by competing with them for carrion, the bodies of dead animals [28,29]. So C. vicina is likely to harm an ecosystem as sensitive as that of the Kerguelen Islands in several ways: by competing with native species, by changing how nutrients move through the ecosystem, and by making it easier for future invaders to arrive [16,27,30,31].

C. vicina was brought to the sub-Antarctic Kerguelen Islands by accident during the 20th century. Long-term monitoring, which began in 1993, has recorded its arrival, its settling in and its spread across the whole group of islands. This gives us a rare chance to understand how the invasion has unfolded, to learn how important this newcomer is in its new home, and to find out why this species is so successful around the world.

The first known sighting of C. vicina in the Kerguelen Islands was in 1978, at Port-aux-Français, the islands' main port and settlement [32]. People suspected the flies had come from Réunion Island, a sub-tropical island. Because conditions on the Kerguelen Islands are so harsh, it was at first thought unlikely that a population able to keep itself going could settle in. A milder climate may have helped the fly settle in about 20 years after it was first recorded there [16]. Before the 1990s, the temperatures at certain times of year may simply not have been high enough for C. vicina to complete its life cycle. However, this has never been properly tested.

C. vicina goes through a complete metamorphosis, meaning its body changes completely as it grows, and it passes through six distinct life stages: egg, three larval instars (the larva grows in steps, shedding its skin each time), pupa (the resting stage in which the larva turns into an adult) and adult (see [33] for a diagram of the life cycle). The female lays her eggs during the day in carrion. The eggs hatch there, and the young larvae feed on the flesh. Once they have fed, the larvae leave the carrion and go to a nearby surface to become pupae. This can happen quickly. Or, if the mother has been exposed to days with short hours of daylight, the third instar larva can enter a resting state controlled by the mother, called diapause, at temperatures below 15 °C in temperate regions [34]. Depending on the conditions, the species can produce one generation per year or several generations per year [35,36,37].

We do not know what effects the C. vicina invasion has on nature. Sub-Antarctic island communities are very easy to invade [16,30], and the Kerguelen ecosystem is unique [32]. So it is essential to understand how this species invaded the Kerguelen Islands and how its invasion has unfolded. With this in mind, our first aim was to find out whether warming could have helped the species settle in the Kerguelen Islands. To do this, we built a degree day model, a calculation that uses the temperatures the fly needs to develop, based on our experiments with this strain of the fly. We then used it to judge whether the years before and after the fly settled in were warm enough for it to complete its life cycle.

Our second aim was to study long-term monitoring records, collected all year round, to look at the timing of C. vicina's seasonal life events in the Kerguelen Islands and how this timing relates to temperature. Knowing how the timing of C. vicina's life events responds to its surroundings helps us understand how this species can keep up with changes in its environment. In turn, this gives us insight into how the invasion has unfolded, how it is likely to develop, and what effects it might have.
parts.methods:
2. Materials and Methods: How We Did the Study

To find out which temperatures C. vicina from the Kerguelen Islands needs in order to develop, we first caught adult flies around the Port-aux-Français research station (49°21′00″ S, 70°13′00″ E) in December 2008 and January 2009. We used traps baited with sheep liver. We then kept these breeding flies in Tupperware® boxes (Nanterre, France) measuring 19 × 19 × 12 cm (length × width × height), with honey, water and a piece of liver where they could lay their eggs.

We placed the newly laid eggs in one of five temperature conditions: 4, 8, 12, 16 or 20 °C. We also kept a control group, which we call the "ambient conditions" (AC) group, at the outdoor temperature. For each temperature, we moved 3–4 groups of 20 eggs, using a small brush, into rearing chambers. There, the eggs sat on raw liver in small boxes that held sand and a piece of damp cotton. From that point on, we checked every day and recorded how many flies were at each stage of growth, until adult flies came out. The one exception was the 4 °C group: its eggs hatched too late to be included in the experiment, after 31 days. We repeated the experiment at least three times for each temperature.

Degree day models predict when a population will reach a particular life stage, such as the adult stage [38]. They do this using a measure called "degree days", which combines heat and time. One degree day is the amount of warmth you would get if you kept an animal at one degree above the lowest temperature at which it can develop for 24 hours. From our temperature experiments, we worked out how many degree days C. vicina needs to reach each stage of its life. We then used these numbers to build a degree day model. With it, we checked whether the warmth built up during the southern summer was enough for the fly to complete its life cycle in the years before and after it settled in on the Kerguelen Islands.

Studies from other regions found that C. vicina can develop at temperatures as low as 1 or 2 °C, depending on how the local populations have adapted (see [39] for a short review). We chose 2 °C as a cautious, low estimate for the lowest temperature at which the fly can develop. Evidence from other regions suggests that the fly cannot develop above 28 °C [26]. We used this upper limit too, although flies on the Kerguelen Islands are unlikely to meet temperatures that high.

We set up our degree day model with three pieces of information: the number of degree days the fly needs to develop, the lowest temperature at which it can develop, and the highest. We counted degree days starting on the 200th day of each calendar year. This date marks the start of the southern winter, before the breeding season. A weather station at the Port-aux-Français research station measured the air temperature for the whole study. Before 2006 it measured the air 2 m above the ground, and from 2006 onwards it measured it 10 cm above the ground.

We also compared the temperature of the soil (5 cm deep) with the air temperature (measured 2 m above the ground). At the time of the study, the two differed very little (project 136-SUBANTECO, French Polar Institute), so we did not adjust the air temperatures to match the soil. We used the model to work out how many days into the breeding season the flies would have built up enough degree days to complete their life cycle. In other words, it showed us which years the flies should be able to survive and breed during the southern summer. We also used a t-test, a common statistical test that checks whether the averages of two groups differ by more than chance alone would usually produce. With it, we compared the number of degree days built up during the southern summer in the years before and after the fly was introduced, to see whether the difference was statistically significant.

We also kept a long-term record of the timing of the adult C. vicina's yearly life events at Port-aux-Français, from 1993 to 2020, using a trap with bait. Adult C. vicina lay their eggs in the bodies of dead animals. These include native seabirds and animals that people brought to the islands: rabbits (Oryctolagus spp., Lilljeborg 1873), mice (Mus spp., Clerck 1757), sheep and mouflons (Ovis spp., Linnaeus 1758), and reindeer (Rangifer tarandus, Linnaeus 1758). The young flies, called larvae, grow in the dead bodies. When they reach their third stage, they move into the soil under the body and turn into pupae, the resting stage before they become adults [40]. So our baited trap held a box with sheep liver (5 cm3) to attract adult C. vicina to lay eggs. We changed the bait about every three months, whenever it had rotted too much.

How often we emptied the trap changed over the years. From 1993 to 1995, we emptied it about every second week from January to June. From 1996 to 1999, we emptied it every second week all year round. From 2000 to 2020, we emptied it every five days from November to April, and every seven to ten days from May to October. After collecting the samples, we sorted them in the laboratory at the Port-aux-Français research station and counted the adult flies. In this study, we used these adult counts to look at the timing of the fly's yearly life events in the area.

To study how the yearly average air temperature changed over time, we used generalised additive models (GAMs). These are statistical tools that fit a smooth, flexible curve through data, so they can follow complicated patterns, such as the ups and downs of temperature, across our seven decades of records [41].

We also recorded C. vicina during general surveys of small animals without backbones on the Kerguelen Islands, from 2004 to 2021. These surveys used several ways of finding and collecting animals. At Port-aux-Français, Isthme-Bas, Guillou Island, Verte Island and Cochons Island, we used pitfall traps, which are cups sunk into the ground so that animals walking past fall in. At Port-aux-Français we also used yellow traps. Across the whole of the Kerguelen Islands, we used soil samples and simply looked for the flies. For each sighting, we wrote down the date and the GPS position (using the WGS 84 map system). We used these records to describe where and when C. vicina was found on the islands.

The places where we saw C. vicina were not the same from year to year, so our records could not show repeated sightings at one particular spot. In the few cases where we did see the fly again at the same place in later years, the point on the map shows when we first saw it there. To map how the area where C. vicina lives changed over time, we used the mapping software QGIS, version 3.22.5 [42].

To see how the timing of adult C. vicina activity changed from year to year, we drew a curve of how many flies were caught over the season for each breeding year (Figure 1). We made these curves with GAMs, using the mgcv package in the statistics program R, version 4.2.1 [43]. We set the models to use a "Poisson distribution", a standard choice for counts, such as the number of flies caught. We did not know the exact shape of the seasonal curve, so we let the model choose a smooth curve that could bend as needed.

We then found the start, peak and end of the activity season. These were the dates by which 10%, 50% and 90% of the total number of adult C. vicina caught that year had been caught (Figure 1). In other words, we added up the area under the curve, which gives the total catch, and found the dates at which each share had been reached. We only included years in which the fly was caught in at least two weeks and in which we could draw a realistic seasonal curve. We left out the years 1994, 2017 and 2020. In 1994 and 2017, we were missing information on the dates when no flies were caught, and in 2020 the curve clearly had two peaks instead of one (Figure S1). We also closed the trap in 2003 and 2015, so we have no data for those years.

Figure 1

An example of how we used generalised additive models to fit a curve to the number of adult blowflies Calliphora vicina caught, to estimate when they started to appear, when they peaked and when they stopped appearing. This example uses the number of C. vicina caught per trap day in 1999–2000. The dashed vertical line marks the start of the calendar year.
parts.results:
3. Results

3.1. How Much Warmth Calliphora vicina Needs to Develop, Based on Flies from the Kerguelen Islands

The temperature at which a fly develops can change several parts of its life cycle. In general, warmer temperatures speed up development, so the fly reaches each stage sooner. In our experiment on how temperature affects development time, we also saw that the early stages were usually shorter than the later ones (Table 1). These were hatching and the first two larval stages, the young worm-like stage of the fly.

From these data, we worked out how many degree days the fly needs to reach each stage (Table 1). We also worked out the total number of degree days needed to complete the whole life cycle. Averaged over all the temperatures we tested, this came to 439 degree days.

Table 1

The number of days from hatching to each stage of the life cycle of Calliphora vicina, and the number of degree days (DD) needed to reach adulthood, for the Kerguelen Islands strain of the fly. The flies were raised at Port-Aux-Français, Kerguelen Islands, at set temperatures (4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 °C) and at the outdoor temperature (ambient conditions, AC). Outdoor temperatures were measured 2 m above the ground by a weather station at Port-Aux-Français. For the calculations, we chose 2 °C as the lowest temperature at which the fly can develop.

| | Days to Stage |

| Temp. (°C) | Hatch | 1st Larval Instar | 2nd Larval Instar | 3rd Larval Instar | Pupa | Adult | Total DD

| 4 | 31 | - | - | - | - | - | -

| 8 | 4.5 | 6 | 9 | 18.5 | 23 | 92.8 | 556.8

| 12 | 2 | 4 | 5 | 7.5 | 12 | 41.5 | 415

| 16 | 1 | 3 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 29.9 | 418.6

| 20 | 1 | 2 | 2.5 | 4 | 5 | 22.6 | 406.8

| AC | 4 | 3 | 4.5 | 10 | 16 | 73 | 397.8

a For each stage, the table shows the median time (in days) from the day the eggs were laid. The median is the middle value when all the results are lined up from shortest to longest. The only exception is 'Hatch', which shows the time until the first 10 percent of the eggs had hatched. Each temperature was tested in at least three separate rearing experiments. b Total degree days were calculated from the median time needed to reach adulthood, counting only temperatures above 2 °C. At a constant temperature, the degree days are the number of days above the 2 °C threshold multiplied by the number of days. For example, at 8 °C the flies took 92.8 days to reach adulthood, so the total was (8 °C–2 °C) × 92.8 = 556.8. The table also lets us work out the degree days needed between two stages in a row. At 8 °C, for example, the flies took 9.5 days (18.5–9) to go from the 2nd to the 3rd larval stage, which means 57 degree days (9.5 × 6).

3.2. How Temperatures on the Kerguelen Islands Have Changed over the Last Seven Decades

Air temperatures on the Kerguelen Islands have generally risen since the 1950s. There was a clear difference between the years before the 1970s and the years after (Figure 2A), and temperatures may have levelled off from then until 2021. The warmest year on record was 2016, with an average air temperature over the year of 5.9 °C. That is 2.2 °C warmer than the coolest year, 1964, when the yearly average was 3.6 °C.

To describe the overall trend, we used a GAM (generalized additive model). This is a statistical method that fits a smooth, flexible curve through the data, so it can follow a trend that bends rather than a straight line. The curve explained 53.8% of the deviance, a measure of how much of the year-to-year variation in temperature the model accounts for. The curve for the year was statistically significant. This means that if temperatures had not really been changing over time, a pattern this strong would rarely appear by chance alone. The curve shows that temperatures rose over the years, but not in a straight line.

Average daily air temperatures jumped around more than average yearly air temperatures. Figure 2B shows an example for 2007–2008. In more recent years, daily temperatures were often above the lowest temperature at which we assume C. vicina can develop (2 °C). The warmest days of each year could add a lot to the degree days that build up quickly for C. vicina.

Figure 2

Temperature trends on the Kerguelen Islands, compared with the degree days that build up and the warmth C. vicina is estimated to need. (A) Average air temperature for each year from 1950 to 2020. The red dashed vertical line marks when C. vicina was first seen on the islands, and the blue vertical line marks when monitoring of the fly began. (B) Daily temperatures in two example years (2007–2008). The grey vertical line marks the start of the calendar year, and the red horizontal line marks the lowest temperature at which we assume the fly can develop (2 °C). (C) Degree days that had built up by the end of the breeding season, worked out from daily temperatures. The season runs from the 200th day of the year (the middle of the southern winter, when adult flies are inactive) to the end of February of the following year. Temperature data come from Météo France.

As temperatures rose, the degree days that built up during the southern summer also increased (Figure 2C). We checked this with a t-test, a common way to compare the averages of two groups of years. The degree days by the end of the southern summer were significantly higher in the years after 1978, when the species was first seen on the islands (Figure 2C; t68 = 4.67, p < 0.0001). The p-value tells us how often a difference this large would turn up by chance alone if there were really no change. Here, that would happen less than 1 time in 10,000. Over the last three decades, the southern summer has almost always brought more than 450 degree days (Figure 2C). This means the fly should have been able to complete its life cycle in most years.

3.3. Long-Term Monitoring of Where and When Calliphora vicina Was Found on the Kerguelen Islands

Our long-term monitoring of where C. vicina lives on the Kerguelen Islands showed that, in the earlier years of sampling (roughly until 2012), the fly was found at many of the places we sampled in the eastern part of the islands. From 2018 onwards, it was found less often (Figure 3 and Figure A1). Large surveys carried out between 2004 and 2007 confirmed that the fly had spread across the eastern part of the islands, including the islands in the Golfe du Morbihan. Flying adults have also been seen on Ile Howe, in the northern part of the islands. In more recent years (2017–2021), the places where the species was found shifted more towards the interior of the Péninsule Courbet (Figure 3).

The number of C. vicina changed a great deal from year to year (Figure A1). The total number caught each year was highest from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s. Between that peak and recent years, the number caught each year fell by about 300 individuals (Figure A1).

Figure 3

Changes in where Calliphora vicina was found on the Kerguelen Islands from 2004 to 2021. Each point shows the period when the fly was first seen. At most places, the species was seen again and again in the periods after it was first found. The map was made in QGIS version 3.22.5, with the sightings plotted on a grid of one-kilometre squares.

3.4. The Timing of the Fly's Yearly Life Events

The time of year when C. vicina was active changed a lot from year to year (Figure 4A). In some years, the flies became active in early January, while in other years they did not become active until April. Activity peaked somewhere between March and early May, and it ended between April and late May. So the flies are active from the southern summer into autumn. This means adult C. vicina are inactive, or very slightly active, in winter. In winter, the adults and the other stages of the fly are probably in a resting state. Since average daily temperatures stay below or around 2 °C in winter (Figure 2B), the fly's development is probably slow or completely stopped during this time.

Figure 4

Estimated timing of the yearly life events of a population of C. vicina on the Kerguelen Islands, based on long-term monitoring data from 1993 to 2019. (A) The period when C. vicina was active in each year from 1993 to 2019. The line shows how long the activity lasted (from start to end), and the points show when activity peaked. (B) The day of the year when the 439 degree days needed for adult C. vicina to emerge had been reached. These degree days were counted from the 200th day of the year, the middle of the southern winter when adult flies are inactive. (C) How the timing of emergence shifted from 1993 to 2019. The grey line and points (bottom) show the start, the light blue line and points (middle) show the peak, and the dark blue line and points (top) show the end. None of the trends were statistically significant.

We also looked closely at the degree days, calculated from hourly temperature records available from 1993 to 2020. The day of the year when enough degree days had built up for adult C. vicina to emerge did not change significantly during the study period (1993–2020) (Figure 4B). In other words, we could not show that this day moved over time. The day when enough warmth had built up varied by a little over a month from year to year. For example, adults emerged on 15 December in 2014 and on 8 November in 2016.

In the same way, our analysis of whether the timing of the fly's yearly life events had changed showed no significant change in the start, peak or end of its activity during 1993–2020 (Figure 4C). For the start, R2 = 0.0008, F1,21 = 0.15, p = 0.90. For the peak, R2 = 0.02, F1,21 = 0.43, p = 0.52. For the end, R2 = 0.01, F1,21 = 0.28, p = 0.60. R2 shows how much of the year-to-year variation a trend line explains, so a value this small means the line explains almost none of it.

Across the years, the peak and the end of emergence were strongly linked to air temperature (Table A1). In other words, both the peak and the end came earlier as temperatures rose. We found no significant effect of air temperature on the start of emergence. Rain and snow were a poor guide to all three of these timing events (Table A1).
parts.discussion:
4. Discussion

When a species is brought to a new place, there is often a delay between the moment it arrives and the moment its numbers start to grow [44,45]. Many different things can cause this delay. Climate change is one of them. As temperatures rise, conditions can change in ways that help "sleeper" populations of newcomers to grow and spread [4]. These are populations that would otherwise survive only in small numbers, or only in small patches where the local weather is milder.

The Kerguelen population of C. vicina is cut off from other populations and lives in a harsh environment that is now changing. This has given us an interesting chance to study how climate change affects the way this newcomer settles in and multiplies. After the first C. vicina was seen in 1978, the flies are thought to have survived inside the heated buildings of the Port-aux-Français research station. New adult flies may also have arrived often, carried by accident on the ships that bring supplies to the station.

In the 1970s, temperatures rose quickly (Figure 3), and this may have made conditions better for C. vicina [16]. We looked at the total amount of warmth built up over the season (degree days). It changed clearly before and after the fly arrived. From the 1980s onwards, the warmth was more than enough for the blowfly to develop. Our study gives evidence that the rising temperatures of this period likely helped the blowfly settle in on the Kerguelen Islands. This then helped it spread through the eastern parts of the islands, where conditions are usually milder.

After settling in, the Kerguelen population of C. vicina may also have slowly become better suited to cool conditions. Unfortunately, we could not test this idea directly. To do so, we would need to compare how well flies from the first arrival phase cope with cold, but nobody ever studied the cold tolerance of the flies brought in the 1970s.

Still, our experiments showed that our flies developed only a little at a low temperature of 4 °C. In other cool regions, however, the flies can come out quickly at even cooler temperatures. For example, one study [46] kept flies collected in Northern England at 3.5 °C, and their eggs hatched in as little as 13 days. Our flies took more than 30 days to hatch at 4 °C. Depending on the region, the lowest temperature at which this species can still develop can be as low as 1 °C (a summary of these lowest temperatures is given in [47]).

The time it took our flies to emerge as adults at 16 °C was also similar to the time taken by flies from Northern Italy raised at 15 °C [26]. This is not conclusive, but it suggests that the Kerguelen population of C. vicina may not yet have adapted to the cooler local conditions. Instead, it is more likely that the species is benefiting from a recent shift towards more favourable temperatures, as our results show.

Our results on the timing of seasonal life events showed that the flies were active during the southern summer (Figure 4A). This is a time of great activity for living things in the area. Being active then gives C. vicina many chances to meet other species in the community. However, future studies that track the timing of many species in the community are needed to understand better how much the fly overlaps in time with the species it interacts with.

C. vicina also seems to be sensitive to a warming climate. As temperatures rose, both the peak and the end of the flies' emergence came earlier, and these shifts were statistically significant (Table A1). A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no link, a pattern this strong would rarely appear by chance alone. This shows that C. vicina benefits from the current changes in climate, and that it should be able to survive if temperatures keep rising on the Kerguelen Islands. Any future benefits from a warmer climate could therefore make its effects on the local community even stronger.

The timing results also showed large differences from year to year in when the flies emerged and how long they stayed active. We also found no statistically significant trend over time in when they emerged. These findings might be explained by the large differences between years, and by the fact that temperature has not changed significantly over time since the late 1980s. Such large differences in timing suggest that this species has a high level of phenotypic plasticity, meaning its body can adjust to changes in climate without any change in its genes. This is often seen in many successful newcomers (for example, [48]). It helps them adjust quickly to new conditions [49], and it lets this species keep pace with shifts in climate more closely than native species can [20].

Climate change is expected to widen the area where many invasive insects like C. vicina can live, and to shorten the time between one generation and the next. For example, climate change may also have helped cause serious outbreaks of the mountain pine beetle (Dendroctonus ponderosae, Hopkins 1902) in North America [50] and of the processionary moth (Thaumetopoea pityocampa, Denis and Schiffermüller 1775) in Europe [51]. When a warming climate shifts the timing of seasonal life events, the growing and breeding seasons may become longer. This can lead to more generations each year, as predicted for the spruce bark beetle (Ips typographus, Linnaeus 1758) in Sweden [52]. Such an increase in the number of generations has already been recorded for the mountain pine beetle (D. ponderosae) in North America [53].

We did not study in detail how many generations C. vicina produces in one season. However, the curves we drew for some of the most recent years (2016, 2017 and 2020) show two peaks in the number of flies across the breeding season (Figure S1). This may suggest that climate change is gradually allowing the flies to produce extra generations by making the breeding season longer. The same has been seen in a number of insects that can adjust easily and produce several generations a year, such as moths and butterflies [54,55].

Our long-term monitoring showed that the Kerguelen C. vicina population seems to go through repeated "boom and bust" cycles, with a period of about two and a half years (Figure A1). In a boom, the numbers rise quickly; in a bust, they crash. Such cycles can be driven by causes found only in newcomer populations, by general ecological causes, or by a mix of several causes [49]. However, our sampling is limited, and without experiments that change conditions on purpose, we cannot identify what causes these cycles.

In summary, our findings show that C. vicina on the Kerguelen Islands must keep being monitored. This will let us follow how the species responds as its breeding seasons grow longer with continued warming. The long-term monitoring on the Kerguelen Islands gives a unique chance to detect changes in the timing of this successful invader's life events and in its numbers as the climate changes. Even so, we still do not know how the response of C. vicina populations to climate change differs from place to place. Future studies could look at how different populations of the same species respond differently to climate change. They could do this by monitoring C. vicina populations from different types of habitat, and by monitoring other life stages, which could respond differently to warming.

In the early 2000s, the future of C. vicina in the sub-Antarctic was less certain. People thought that several cold years in a row could wipe out the local population by stopping the flies from developing (136-SUBANTECO, French Polar Institute). However, those cold years in a row never came, and C. vicina survived. People are always present on the Kerguelen Islands, so goods must keep being brought in by supply ships. This means C. vicina is likely to be brought back quickly, even if the population were to disappear completely. Together with average temperatures that keep rising and the species' quick response to warming, this means the fly is likely "here to stay" on the Kerguelen Islands. So we need to understand better how important this species is as an invader on the Kerguelen Islands, so that its effects can be managed.

The effects of the C. vicina invasion on the ecosystem have rarely been studied. Even so, we have identified at least three main ways in which C. vicina could change how nature works on the Kerguelen Islands. These are (i) its use of carrion (the bodies of dead animals), (ii) its possible role as food for other species, and (iii) its possible role as a pollinator, or, because it is a strong flier, as a carrier of seeds and other plant parts that could help plants from elsewhere settle in and spread.

The first of these, C. vicina as a carrion eater, could affect the local ecosystem in several ways. For example, C. vicina larvae (maggots) may compete with other carrion eaters, such as Anatalanta aptera (Eaton 1875), a wingless fly found nowhere else. Similar competition has been seen in other pairs of native and newcomer carrion blowflies [29]. However, experiments by Chevrier, Vernon and Frenot [27] showed that these two species do not compete directly when food is plentiful. Indirect competition may still happen, though. Some blowflies can time their arrival at carrion so that they do not arrive at the same time as others, or they can avoid carrion that is already taken. This reduces direct competition and also the risk of being eaten by a predator that shares the same food [56,57]. Compared with A. aptera, C. vicina develops fast and is better at spreading to new places. This could let it reach carrion more easily and use it, and it could possibly push A. aptera out, especially where carrion is scarce [16]. Together with threats from other newcomers, such as the predatory beetle Merizodus soledadinus (Guérin-Méneville 1830), this could put the long-term survival of A. aptera at risk [16,58].

Disease-causing germs (pathogens) can also pass from one animal to another through shared material such as carrion [59]. This could lead to "spillover" and "spillback" [60,61,62], involving pathogens or parasites that come from C. vicina, from other decomposers, or from both. Spillover happens when a pathogen or parasite "spills" from one population into another. Spillback happens when the newly infected population then becomes a source of the pathogen for the original population that carried it [8]. Other blowflies have been shown to spread pathogens such as anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) from carcasses to the surrounding environment and plants [60], and C. vicina could also affect how pathogens spread locally.

In addition, carrion-eating C. vicina larvae could affect the wider ecosystem by changing the small-scale conditions inside the carrion and the speed at which nutrients are recycled. Blowfly larvae can create a "larval mass effect": when many larvae gather together, they warm up the carrion. This may help them survive in two ways. First, higher temperatures make them grow fast, so they spend less time in a stage of life when they are easily harmed [63], especially in places where temperatures are fairly low. Second, higher temperatures may give C. vicina an advantage over competing species [64]. Warmer carrion could also make conditions better for tiny decomposers and speed up decay, which would change how nutrients are recycled.

The second main way the C. vicina invasion could affect the local community is by becoming new food for predators, such as the invasive house mouse (Mus musculus) and the predatory ground beetle M. soledadinus, especially when the flies are larvae. Once C. vicina becomes an adult, it is unlikely to be important food for any local species. This is because no predator in the community is adapted to catching insects in the air, since there are no native flying insects on the Kerguelen Islands. C. vicina could also become food for newcomers in the future, helping them settle in, multiply and spread across the region.

Finally, besides possibly changing how dead animals decay and serving as food, C. vicina could affect the local ecosystem by helping plants that depend on pollinators to invade in the future [65]. Many sub-Antarctic islands have no pollinating insects, and most native plants are pollinated by the wind. Adult C. vicina visit flowers and drink nectar. So large numbers of these flies give insect-pollinated plants a chance to settle in, spread and multiply in future sub-Antarctic communities [32,65]. Through its possible links with other species, as food or as a pollinator, C. vicina could help many different species invade and add to an "invasional meltdown" on the Kerguelen Islands [8,66]. This is a situation in which one invader helps other invaders, so that invasions build on each other and become harder to control.
